title: Michael J. Fox Earns 18th Emmy Nomination After Parkinson's-Defying Return to Acting
excerpt: The Back to the Future star came out of retirement to play a Parkinson's patient on Apple TV's Shrinking, earning his first Emmy nomination since 2016 and calling the experience life-sustaining.
body:
Five years after announcing his retirement from acting, Michael J. Fox is back — and the Television Academy has noticed. The 65-year-old actor earned his 18th career Emmy nomination this month for his guest-starring role on Apple TV's Shrinking, a comeback that he says has been as therapeutic as it has been creative.

The Return

Fox stepped away from acting in 2020 as Parkinson's disease — which he was diagnosed with at age 29 in 1991 — made memorising lines increasingly difficult. In his memoir No Time Like the Future, he wrote that "not being able to speak reliably is a game-breaker for an actor."

https://x.com/californiapost/status/2080052365907071377

The door reopened when Bill Lawrence, co-creator of Shrinking and Fox's former collaborator on Spin City in the late 1990s, wrote a role with Fox specifically in mind. Fox plays Gerry, a Parkinson's patient who befriends Harrison Ford's character Paul Rhoades, a therapist who is also navigating a Parkinson's diagnosis.

The result is something Fox described as unprecedented in his career: the first time he has played a character interacting with another person who has Parkinson's on screen. "I discovered this new niche," Fox told CinemaBlend, describing how he had previously channelled his symptoms into roles depicting cancer and other conditions. But Shrinking let him be direct about it.

"It was hell on Tracy, it was really hard on her — and it still is because it's always changing. I said to her, 'I have to go all the way here. No half measures.'"

— Michael J. Fox, on his wife Tracy Pollan, to The Hollywood Reporter

A Career Built on Resilience

Fox's trajectory is one of Hollywood's most remarkable stories of adaptation. After rocketing to fame with Back to the Future in 1985 and winning three Emmys for Family Ties, he was privately diagnosed with Parkinson's at 29. He continued acting for seven years before disclosing his condition publicly in 1998.

He left Spin City in 2000 and founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research that same year. The foundation has since funded $3 billion in research, making it the largest private funder of Parkinson's science worldwide, according to Entertainment Weekly.

Fox continued taking on occasional roles — including his acclaimed recurring turn as attorney Louis Canning on The Good Wife and its spinoff The Good Fight — before his second retirement in 2020. His 2023 Apple TV documentary Still offered an unflinching look at his daily reality with the disease.

The Emmy Recognition

Fox's nomination in the Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series category is his first since 2016 and his 18th overall. He has won five Emmys across his career — three for Family Ties, one for Spin City, and one for a guest role on Rescue Me in 2009.

Ford also received a nomination for Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series for his portrayal of Rhoades, meaning both actors depicting Parkinson's on the show are in Emmy contention — a first for any television series.

Lawrence, who has said Fox was his "first mentor" in television, told People that he wanted to "represent it in hopefully an inspiring and not sad or tragic way." The Parkinson's storyline was also personal for Lawrence: both his father and Shrinking co-creator Brett Goldstein's father have the disease.

What It Means

Fox has been candid about the toll Parkinson's takes on his family. "It's getting harder. Every day, it's tougher," he said in a CBS interview. He has broken multiple bones from falls — both arms, an elbow, his hand, and his face — and has undergone spinal surgery for a benign tumour.

Yet the return to work appears to have been restorative. Fox told The Hollywood Reporter that he needed to "normalize" his condition publicly. "I have to not hide this. F--- vanity," he said.

His philosophy, distilled in his own words: "Gratitude feeds optimism." For the millions worldwide living with Parkinson's — and for their families — Fox's continued presence on screen carries weight that extends well beyond entertainment.
